sentences.text: Krabisuchus possessed a short, blunt snout where the front part was roughly as long as the back of the head from the eye sockets.
The skull is described as relatively deep, a condition known as altirostry.
The nasal bones are very wide, making up one-third of the maximum snout width.
This animal had large eyes and a small skull table located much higher than the snout.
Fossils of Krabisuchus have been found in the Krabi Basin of southern Thailand.
The material was recovered between 1989 and 1994 by French and Thai scientists led by Varavudh Suteethorn and Eric Buffetaut.
Krabisuchus was first named by paleontologists Jeremy A. Martin and Komsorn Lauprasert in 2010.
The type species of Krabisuchus is K. siamogallicus.
The terrestrial environment where Krabisuchus lived is generally interpreted as a closed, densely vegetated subtropical to tropical forest.
Evidence for a forested habitat includes the presence of diverse arboreal fauna such as colugos, primates, and flying foxes.
The presence of the fully terrestrial plant Magnolia champaca suggests that the forests of the Krabi Basin were terrestrial rather than mangrove swamps.
Like other extinct alligatorines, Krabisuchus was probably more terrestrial than semiaquatic.
Krabisuchus was originally classified as a member of the group Alligatoroidea.
A 2014 study by Skutschas and colleagues recovered Krabisuchus as a basal member of Alligatoridae in a polytomy with Allognathosuchus, Hassiacosuchus, Navajosuchus, and the Maoming alligator.
In the description of Jiangxisuchus, Li and colleagues recovered Krabisuchus as an early member of the subfamily Caimaninae.
Krabisuchus is known exclusively from Late Eocene sediments found in the Krabi Basin of southern Thailand.
The fossil-bearing sediments of the Krabi Basin consist of ancient river deposits, a primary coal seam, and overlying lake deposits.
Krabisuchus lived during the Eocene epoch.
The time range for Krabisuchus is from 37.71 to 33.9 million years ago.
The affinities of the clade Orientalosuchina are disputed.
Tobias Massonne and his team argued that features initially interpreted as sutures in Krabisuchus were actually pre-orbital ridges.
It is debated whether the placement of Krabisuchus within Alligatoroidea is supported by all phylogenetic studies.
It is debated whether a longirostrine crocodilian previously referred to Eosuchus should be classified in the genus Maomingosuchus rather than Krabisuchus.
